references.abstract: Abstract State of health diagnosis and estimation of lithium-ion batteries is a key feature of an advanced battery management system. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy is frequently used for the state of health diagnosis and estimation. In the paper, the charge transfer resistance of the battery is obtained by fitting the impedance spectroscopy with an equivalent impedance model to estimate state of health. And an analytical calculation model with temperature and state of charge as inputs is derived and verified considering their effect on the charge transfer resistance. With the calculation model, the charge transfer resistance at randomly selected state of charge and temperature is converted to the standard state to be comparable for the state of health estimation. It is indicated that state of health estimated with the converted and the direct fitted charge transfer resistance agree well. The battery state of health estimation method with the converted charge transfer resistance eliminates the need to specifically control the temperature and state of charge during the impedance spectrum measurement. It benefits the practical application of the state of health estimation with electrochemical impedance spectroscopy.

problem: For one lithium-ion cell chemistry and two controlled aging protocols, can EIS measurements limited to a predefined rapid frequency band estimate capacity-based state of health (SOH) across specified temperature and state-of-charge (SOC) ranges, and identify loss of lithium inventory (LLI) versus loss of active material (LAM) only when supported by independent reference diagnostics? Evaluate performance on cells and one aging protocol excluded from training, against full-spectrum EIS, SOH-only EIS models, and established voltage/current or incremental-capacity diagnostics. Does prediction uncertainty remain calibrated on these held-out data, as measured by coverage of prespecified prediction intervals?
problem_rationale: The target review calls for stronger links between EIS, aging mechanisms, and practical SOH estimation. Prior studies establish fast EIS acquisition, temperature/SOC compensation, and impedance-based SOH prediction; other work compares EIS with incremental-capacity and differential-voltage analysis for diagnosing degradation. The proposed study brings these threads together but narrows the scope to make the claims testable: one chemistry, two aging protocols, a predefined measurement band and operating envelope, and validation on unseen cells and a protocol. Capacity measurements provide the SOH reference, while independent diagnostic evidence provides LLI/LAM labels. Because degradation mechanisms can coexist or be indistinguishable from partial EIS, the model should report a mode only when reference-supported labels and measurement evidence permit it, otherwise returning “ambiguous.” Comparing with full-spectrum and established diagnostic baselines will show the cost of faster measurements; prediction-interval coverage on held-out data will test whether reported uncertainty is reliable beyond the training conditions.

Clarity.review: The problem is clearly framed as a bounded, testable study. It specifies the cell chemistry scope, aging protocols, rapid EIS constraint, operating conditions, capacity-based SOH target, degradation-mode distinction, held-out validation, comparison baselines, and uncertainty-calibration measure. The rationale connects these choices to the cited research landscape and appropriately recognizes that partial-spectrum EIS may not distinguish coexisting degradation mechanisms.
Clarity.feedback: Clarify what “predefined rapid frequency band” means, including its frequency limits and how the band is selected. Define the capacity-based SOH formula and the reference diagnostics used to label LLI and LAM. Also specify what “one aging protocol excluded from training” means for the split and whether results must generalize to both held-out cells and that protocol. Finally, identify the prediction-interval levels and the criterion for acceptable calibration. These details would make the evaluation more reproducible without changing the problem’s scope.

Relevance.review: The problem is strongly relevant to current EIS-based battery health research. It connects directly to work on rapid impedance acquisition, temperature/SOC effects, SOH prediction, and comparisons with incremental-capacity and voltage-based diagnostics. Its focus on held-out cells and an unseen aging protocol addresses a meaningful limitation of many estimation studies: performance that does not generalize beyond the training data. Separating capacity-based SOH evaluation from mechanism labels supported by independent diagnostics is also appropriately cautious, particularly given that partial-band EIS may not uniquely distinguish LLI from LAM.
Relevance.feedback: The scope is well defined and the proposed baselines make the practical trade-off between measurement speed and diagnostic performance testable. Specify the frequency band and acquisition-time target in advance, and define how cells and protocols are split to prevent leakage. Prespecify the uncertainty-calibration metric and acceptable coverage tolerance, alongside point-prediction metrics. Also clarify which independent diagnostics establish LLI/LAM labels and how mixed or uncertain labels are handled. These details will make the claims about generalization, mechanism identification, and calibrated uncertainty more interpretable.

Originality.review: The problem is well grounded in the cited literature and is more specific than a general proposal for EIS-based SOH estimation. Fast EIS acquisition, temperature/SOC effects, impedance-based prediction, and comparisons with incremental-capacity or voltage-differential methods have all been studied. The potentially distinctive contribution is to test a predefined rapid frequency band under protocol-held-out validation, pair capacity-based SOH with independently supported degradation labels, allow an “ambiguous” mechanism outcome, and assess prediction-interval calibration on held-out data. These choices make the study’s claims more rigorous and practically relevant, though they appear to be a careful synthesis and evaluation of established directions rather than a clearly unprecedented research question.
Originality.feedback: Specify how the rapid frequency band and operating envelope will be selected without using held-out data, and define the independent diagnostics and criteria used to assign LLI/LAM labels or mark cases ambiguous. Clarify the number and diversity of cells, how the excluded protocol tests generalization rather than a protocol-specific shift, and which baselines will be matched for training data and tuning. Prespecify calibration metrics and interval construction; empirical coverage alone can be misleading without interval width and adequate held-out sample size. These details will determine whether the combined validation design yields a substantive contribution beyond prior fast-EIS and degradation-diagnosis studies.

Feasibility.review: The problem is well scoped and experimentally testable. Its aims are supported by the cited research directions: rapid EIS acquisition, operating-condition compensation, SOH prediction, and comparison with established degradation diagnostics. Limiting the study to one chemistry, two aging protocols, and a predefined temperature/SOC envelope makes the data collection and validation more manageable. Capacity provides a clear SOH reference, while the requirement for independent diagnostics appropriately limits claims about LLI and LAM. Held-out cells and an entirely held-out protocol offer a meaningful test of generalization, and prediction-interval coverage adds a concrete check on uncertainty calibration.
Feasibility.feedback: The main feasibility risks are access to enough cells and the time and cost required to age them, especially if one complete protocol is reserved for testing. Specify the cell count, aging endpoints, EIS band and acquisition conditions, independent reference methods for labeling LLI/LAM, and the criteria for returning “ambiguous.” Ensure the baselines receive comparable training data and operating-condition information. Calibrating prediction intervals on a sufficiently large calibration set may be difficult when the test protocol is genuinely unseen; prespecify how calibration will be assessed and avoid implying that coverage on one held-out protocol establishes broad reliability. The proposed work is feasible, but its strength will depend on experimental replication and disciplined limits on mechanism claims.

Significance.review: The problem is significant and well grounded in the EIS battery-diagnostics literature. It addresses a practical obstacle to deploying EIS for battery management: whether faster, limited-band measurements can deliver reliable SOH estimates across operating conditions and generalize to unseen cells and aging protocols. Its comparison with full-spectrum EIS and established diagnostics makes the speed–accuracy tradeoff assessable. The cautious treatment of LLI/LAM, including an “ambiguous” outcome when evidence is insufficient, also avoids overstating what impedance data can establish. Calibrated prediction intervals add useful evidence about reliability beyond average prediction error.
Significance.feedback: The scope is appropriately constrained, but the contribution depends on clearly defining the frequency band, temperature/SOC envelope, cell-level and protocol-level data splits, and the independent diagnostics used to assign LLI/LAM labels. Specify interval-coverage targets and how coverage will be assessed; with limited held-out data, apparent calibration may be imprecise. Also clarify whether “unseen protocol” means an entire protocol is held out, since that is a stronger generalization test than holding out cells from protocols represented in training. These details will determine whether the results support practical deployment or only feasibility for the tested chemistry and conditions.

method:
** Define the study’s scope before enrollment: one named cell chemistry and format, two controlled aging protocols, a fixed temperature/SOC envelope, and a rapid EIS band. Select that band using an engineering rule independent of SOH and mechanism outcomes: identify a contiguous frequency range that the intended instrument can acquire within a prespecified time limit and that spans the targeted electrochemical processes, using pilot or published data only. Freeze the band, acquisition settings, preprocessing, and analysis plan before collecting study outcomes. Treat findings as applying to this chemistry, format, instrument class, and operating envelope.

Use a randomized, blocked design with cells from at least two manufacturing batches allocated across both protocols, so protocol is not confounded with batch. Set cell counts by simulation-based power and precision analysis using the cell—not each measurement—as the independent unit; choose counts to estimate the primary SOH error and interval coverage with prespecified confidence-interval widths, and ensure enough independently reference-labeled cells for mechanism evaluation. Report the assumptions and resulting allocation in the preregistration. If only two protocols are feasible, describe protocol transfer as a test between these two conditions, not evidence of broad transfer to other aging regimes.

At fixed aging checkpoints, acquire rapid-band and full-spectrum EIS on the same cells. Preregister the frequency grid and perturbation settings for both measurements, temperature/SOC grid, and a maximum acquisition time for the rapid band. For each condition, equilibrate until cell temperature is within ±0.5 °C of target and open-circuit voltage changes by less than a prespecified threshold over a fixed monitoring window; record failures to reach equilibrium. Randomize measurement order where feasible, standardize rest periods, and repeat a subset to quantify repeatability. Accept spectra only when instrument-range checks pass and a preregistered linearity/stability and Kramers–Kronig residual criterion is met. Retain failed or missing observations in the study flow and report their reasons; do not impute failed spectra as valid measurements.

Define capacity-based SOH as measured discharge capacity divided by the cell’s initial reference capacity, under a fixed temperature, current, voltage limits, and rest procedure. Measure reference capacity at baseline and each checkpoint, with replicate tests at a prespecified subset of checkpoints to quantify reference error.

Assign mechanism labels without using EIS model outputs. Use a preregistered combination of reference diagnostics, such as half-cell electrode balancing from harvested cells, supported where available by coulombic-efficiency and differential-voltage/incremental-capacity analysis. State the diagnostic protocol, fitting procedure, uncertainty, and evidence threshold in advance. Classify cases as LLI-dominant or LAM-dominant only when the relevant diagnostic evidence exceeds that threshold and uncertainty excludes the competing interpretation; label co-occurring supported mechanisms as mixed, and insufficient or conflicting evidence as indeterminate. Evaluate classification performance only against determinate reference labels, while reporting mixed, indeterminate, and model-ambiguous fractions separately.

Separate data at the cell level before any feature selection or tuning. The primary transfer test uses the second aging protocol as a completely held-out protocol, with its cells excluded from fitting, feature selection, calibration, and threshold setting. Also reserve cells from the training protocol as a distinct held-out-cell test. Thus report two separate tests: new cells under a represented protocol, and a new protocol. If protocol and cohort differences remain inseparable, state that limitation. Use the training data only for model selection and threshold setting; use nested cell-grouped cross-validation within the training protocol for tuning.

For the rapid-band SOH model, use a preregistered, regularized hierarchical regression with temperature and SOC as covariates, cell-level random effects during training, and a fixed-effects prediction rule for unseen cells. Transform real and imaginary impedance components to log-magnitude/phase or a preregistered equivalent representation, standardize using training data only, and retain the same preprocessing for all EIS models. Construct 90% and 95% prediction intervals using a cell-grouped conformal calibration procedure on training data; do not recalibrate on held-out data. Report empirical coverage and interval width with cell-clustered confidence intervals, overall and by temperature, SOC, protocol, and SOH range. Include residual and calibration plots, but treat prespecified coverage estimates and their uncertainty as the calibration assessment.

Train a separate mechanism model only on determinate reference-labeled cases. Make an LLI or LAM call only if the predicted class probability exceeds a threshold fixed on training data and the corresponding reference-supported evidence condition is met; otherwise return “ambiguous.” Never force mixed or indeterminate references into a binary class. Report sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, and confusion matrices on determinate cases, alongside the proportion of all test cases called, mixed, indeterminate, or ambiguous.

Compare the rapid-band models with full-spectrum EIS models, SOH-only EIS models, and voltage/current and incremental-capacity/differential-voltage baselines. Give each baseline the same training cells, tuning budget, reference outcomes, and held-out splits; prohibit access to held-out labels or measurements during model selection. Prespecify primary SOH performance as cell-weighted mean absolute error, with RMSE and signed bias as secondary metrics. Aggregate repeated checkpoint measurements within cells for inferential uncertainty using cell-clustered bootstrap intervals, and report checkpoint-level results as descriptive rather than treating observations as independent. Report missingness and all exclusions by split.

**
method_rationale:
** The protocol specifies the acquisition conditions, references, modeling, split logic, and decision rules needed to reproduce the study and interpret its claims. Selecting the rapid band by an outcome-independent time-and-process rule avoids choosing frequencies because they happen to predict this dataset’s SOH. Batch blocking and separate held-out-cell and held-out-protocol tests help distinguish transfer to new cells from transfer across the two tested aging conditions, while acknowledging that two protocols cannot establish general transfer.

Capacity provides an independent SOH target. Mechanism labels come from diagnostics independent of the EIS model, with uncertainty and mixed or indeterminate cases preserved; this limits circular validation and makes the scope of mechanism claims explicit. The hierarchical model addresses operating-condition and cell variation, while cell-grouped conformal intervals provide a prespecified way to assess uncertainty without calibrating on the test data. Matched baselines and cell-level inference make the rapid-band trade-off and its uncertainty measurable. Conclusions remain limited to the tested chemistry, format, equipment class, and operating envelope; extension to other chemistries, manufacturers, or field duty cycles requires external validation.

Clarity.review: The method is clearly structured and addresses the central risks in the research problem: outcome-independent frequency-band selection, cell-level data splitting, independent SOH and mechanism references, held-out testing, matched baselines, and explicit uncertainty assessment. Its scope is appropriately limited to the tested chemistry, format, protocols, and operating envelope. The steps are detailed enough to understand the intended study and its main comparisons, but some operational and statistical choices remain underspecified for direct replication.
Clarity.feedback: Specify the chemistry and cell format, aging protocol parameters, frequency limits and grid, EIS perturbation and acquisition settings, and temperature/SOC ranges before enrollment. Several criteria are deferred to preregistration without indicating how they will be chosen: the equilibration thresholds and window, spectral acceptance limits, mechanism evidence thresholds, model specification and feature representation, and conformal calibration procedure. Define these choices, including how reference diagnostics are obtained and how destructive testing is handled. Clarify the split structure: if one of only two protocols is entirely held out, explain how training-protocol cells are divided between model development and held-out-cell evaluation, and ensure the latter does not inform tuning or calibration. Also state how interval calibration handles repeated observations and clustered cells, and how SOH-only EIS models differ from the primary model. These details would make the protocol more reproducible and the reported comparisons easier to interpret.

Validity.review: The method is well aligned with the research problem and addresses the main validity risks: outcome-independent frequency-band selection, independent SOH and mechanism references, cell-level separation, a genuinely held-out protocol, matched baselines, and explicit uncertainty assessment. Its claims are appropriately bounded to the tested chemistry, format, equipment, and operating conditions. The design also recognizes that two protocols support only a limited transfer test, not broad generalization.
Validity.feedback:
Several details need tightening before the protocol is fully reproducible. First, clarify the held-out-protocol design: if only two protocols are used, training on one and testing on the other leaves protocol transfer confounded with protocol identity and potentially cohort or batch effects. Blocking batches across protocols helps, but the analysis should specify how batch representation is maintained and how this limitation will be handled. Second, define the prediction target and evaluation unit precisely: repeated checkpoints from the same cell are correlated, and cell-weighted MAE should state how checkpoint errors are aggregated so cells with more valid measurements do not receive disproportionate weight.

Specify the hierarchical model’s structure and how its fixed-effects prediction for unseen cells handles cell-level random effects. Also clarify that conformal coverage guarantees depend on exchangeability; calibration from one protocol may not yield valid coverage on the held-out protocol. Report protocol-specific coverage as an empirical test, without implying distribution-free guarantees under protocol shift. Finally, define the frequency-selection evidence for “spans the targeted electrochemical processes,” the Kramers–Kronig acceptance criterion, mechanism diagnostic thresholds, and the “reference-supported evidence condition” used by the mechanism model. These choices are central to reproducibility and should be fixed before outcome analysis.

Rigorousness.review: The method is unusually well structured and closely aligned with the research question. It defines the scope and measurement conditions, separates training from cell- and protocol-level tests, uses independent capacity and mechanism references, and prespecifies comparisons, outcomes, and uncertainty assessment. It also appropriately limits claims to the tested chemistry and two protocols, and preserves mixed, indeterminate, and ambiguous mechanism cases rather than forcing binary conclusions.
Rigorousness.feedback: Several details need to be resolved before the protocol is fully reproducible. The proposed hierarchical model includes cell-level random effects during training, but the fixed-effects prediction rule for unseen cells needs a precise specification, including how uncertainty from new-cell variability is represented. Conformal coverage is not automatically guaranteed under a held-out protocol shift; state the exchangeability assumptions, define the calibration unit and interval construction for repeated checkpoints, and interpret held-out coverage as an empirical test rather than a guarantee. Clarify whether the second protocol is held out entirely or whether any of its cells can enter calibration; the current split description implies it is entirely excluded, so calibration must use training-protocol data only. Also specify the mechanism-diagnostic evidence thresholds and how destructive diagnostics on harvested cells will be linked to checkpoint-level predictions. Finally, define the SOH-only EIS comparator, ensure the rapid-band/full-spectrum comparisons use appropriately matched modeling choices, and prespecify how repeated measurements and multiple temperature/SOC conditions contribute to cell-weighted metrics and confidence intervals. These refinements would reduce ambiguity without changing the study’s core design.

Innovativeness.review:
The method is carefully designed and substantially improves the rigor of a rapid-EIS evaluation. Its strongest contribution is the combination of a frequency band selected independently of outcomes, genuinely held-out cell and protocol tests, mechanism labels established without EIS model outputs, and explicit evaluation of prediction-interval coverage. Together, these choices make the central claims more testable and reduce common sources of leakage, circular validation, and overstatement.

The individual techniques are largely established rather than novel: impedance acquisition and modeling, capacity-based SOH, diagnostic comparisons, hierarchical regression, and conformal calibration are known approaches. The main innovation is their integration into a preregistered, scope-limited evaluation that distinguishes new-cell performance from transfer between two protocols. The design is rigorous, but it is not a new measurement principle or modeling method, and testing only two protocols limits the strength of any generalization claim.
Innovativeness.feedback: Make the primary estimand and analysis unit especially explicit: repeated observations are clustered within cells, so define how cell-weighted error and uncertainty are calculated across checkpoints and operating conditions. Clarify how conformal calibration is performed with cell-grouped data and what coverage guarantee, if any, is expected under the dependence structure; empirical held-out coverage is informative but does not by itself establish calibration beyond the tested distribution. Also specify how many cells can receive independent mechanism labels, since harvested-cell diagnostics may not support labels at every checkpoint, and how this sampling affects the mechanism analysis. Keep conclusions about protocol transfer narrowly tied to the two tested protocols.

Generalizability.review: The method is carefully designed to test transfer beyond the training cells and one aging protocol, while keeping its claims tied to the tested chemistry, format, instrument class, and operating envelope. Cell-level splits, batch blocking, independent mechanism references, and matched baselines make the proposed generalizability assessment substantially stronger than a random measurement-level split. Still, the scope is intentionally narrow: testing only two controlled protocols does not establish transfer to other aging regimes, and no external chemistry, manufacturer, format, instrument, or field data are included. The method therefore evaluates limited, well-defined forms of transfer rather than broad applicability.
Generalizability.feedback: Preserve the distinction between held-out-cell and held-out-protocol performance, and avoid describing success on two protocols as general protocol transfer. Report whether the held-out protocol differs in only the intended aging condition or also in cohort, batch, or calendar time; otherwise, the source of any transfer failure will be hard to interpret. Clarify how destructive reference diagnostics from harvested cells map to the labeled test population, since selective harvesting or incomplete labels could limit mechanism-model generalizability. Finally, treat conformal coverage as conditional on the calibration and test data being exchangeable: a held-out protocol may violate that assumption, so coverage should be interpreted as an empirical test of transfer, not guaranteed by the procedure. External validation across chemistries, manufacturers, formats, and field duty cycles would be needed before making broader claims.

experiment:
Conduct a preregistered laboratory study of one commercial cell type, specified before enrollment by chemistry, form factor, manufacturer, model, and lot. Use two aging protocols with explicit current, voltage limits, temperature, rest, and cycling conditions. Draw cells from at least two manufacturing batches and allocate each batch across both protocols where available. Freeze the operating envelope, measurement procedures, analysis code, and decision criteria before outcome collection. The study’s conclusions will apply only to this cell type and the two tested protocols.

Set the sample size using a simulation-based precision analysis, treating cells as independent sampling units and checkpoints as repeated observations. The preregistration must give the assumed between-cell variation, within-cell correlation, expected attrition and indeterminate-label rate, target confidence-interval widths, and resulting allocation by batch, protocol, and split. As an operational starting point, plan for 120 cells: 60 per protocol, with 40 per protocol assigned to training and 20 per protocol held out by cell. The protocol-2 cells remain completely excluded from model fitting, feature selection, calibration, and threshold selection; their 40 cells form the held-out-protocol test. The 20 protocol-1 holdout cells form the new-cell test. Final enrollment must be increased if the preregistered simulation shows this allocation cannot meet the primary precision target. Mechanism classification is confirmatory only if each held-out test has at least 20 determinate reference cases per class; otherwise report classification estimates and uncertainty as exploratory, without claiming adequate validation.

Before enrollment, pilot the complete measurement sequence on non-study cells. Use published or pilot information, without SOH or mechanism outcomes, to select a contiguous rapid frequency band that covers the intended electrochemical processes and meets a fixed acquisition-time limit. Preregister the exact frequency grids, instrument model and calibration, perturbation amplitude, number of cycles or averaging rule, and acquisition settings for rapid and full-spectrum EIS. Also preregister the temperature and SOC grid, rest periods, equilibration monitoring window, and numerical quality-control criteria. For example, require cell temperature within ±0.5 °C and a preregistered maximum open-circuit-voltage drift before measurement; specify numerical limits for instrument range, linearity/stability, and Kramers–Kronig residuals. Record all failed measurements and their reasons. Randomize rapid/full-spectrum measurement order where feasible and repeat a prespecified subset to estimate repeatability.

At baseline and fixed aging checkpoints, acquire rapid-band and full-spectrum EIS on each cell at the specified temperature/SOC conditions. Measure reference discharge capacity at baseline and each checkpoint using fixed temperature, current, voltage limits, and rest procedure. Define SOH as checkpoint capacity divided by that cell’s baseline capacity. Replicate capacity tests at a prespecified subset of checkpoints to estimate reference-measurement error. Keep the checkpoint schedule manageable and report instrument-hours, cycler capacity, expected attrition, and completed measurements by split.

Use independent diagnostics for mechanism labels. Randomly select cells for destructive testing within batch, protocol, and checkpoint strata, with the selection schedule fixed before outcomes are examined. At the selected checkpoint, perform electrode balancing on harvested cells using a preregistered half-cell procedure, fitting method, uncertainty calculation, and quantitative evidence thresholds. For non-harvested cells and unmeasured checkpoints, do not assign a definitive label by assuming the harvested subset represents them; use only preregistered non-destructive supporting diagnostics where their evidence meets the same criteria, or label the case indeterminate. Use coulombic efficiency and incremental-capacity/differential-voltage evidence as supporting diagnostics, not substitutes for the independent reference where the protocol requires harvest confirmation. Label LLI-dominant or LAM-dominant only when the relevant estimate exceeds its threshold and its uncertainty excludes the competing interpretation; label supported co-occurrence as mixed and insufficient or conflicting evidence as indeterminate. Report how labels were obtained and the fraction of cases in each category.

Split data by cell before any feature selection, scaling, tuning, calibration, or threshold setting. Within protocol 1 training cells, use nested cell-grouped cross-validation. Train a regularized hierarchical regression on preregistered rapid-band features, such as log magnitude and phase at fixed frequencies, with temperature and SOC covariates. Estimate preprocessing parameters from training data only; use fixed-effects predictions for unseen cells. Define the SOH-only EIS comparator as an EIS model without temperature or SOC covariates, using the same EIS inputs, preprocessing, splits, and tuning budget. Define the full-spectrum comparator using the same model family and fitting procedure but the preregistered full frequency grid. Define voltage/current and incremental-capacity/differential-voltage baselines with fixed feature extraction and equivalent access to training outcomes and tuning effort.

Calibrate 90% and 95% prediction intervals using cell-grouped conformal calibration on protocol-1 training data only. The calibration unit must be the cell, not the checkpoint: aggregate or otherwise define each cell’s calibration score in advance so repeated observations do not inflate the calibration sample size. State the exchangeability assumption and treat held-out-protocol coverage as a test under possible distribution shift, not as guaranteed by conformal theory. Do not recalibrate on either holdout. Report coverage and interval width with cell-clustered confidence intervals overall; subgroup results by temperature, SOC, protocol, and SOH range are exploratory when cell counts are insufficient for informative intervals.

Train the LLI/LAM classifier only on determinate reference-labeled training cases. Fix its probability threshold using training data alone. Make a class call only when the threshold is met and the applicable independent diagnostic evidence supports that label; otherwise return “ambiguous.” Never force mixed or indeterminate references into a binary class. Report sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, confusion matrices, and the fractions called, ambiguous, mixed, and indeterminate.

Prespecify cell-weighted MAE as the primary SOH metric; report RMSE and signed bias as secondary metrics. Compare rapid-band performance with each baseline on the same held-out cells and protocol. Set a practical-use criterion before enrollment: define the maximum acceptable MAE from the intended application’s SOH tolerance, and define the largest acceptable MAE increase versus full-spectrum EIS as the cost allowed for faster acquisition. Report confidence intervals for these differences using cell-clustered bootstrap resampling. If the study lacks precision to establish these criteria, report the estimates and uncertainty without declaring the rapid method practically equivalent or useful. Report exclusions, missingness, quality-control failures, acquisition time, and cell flow for every split.
experiment_rationale:
This protocol makes the key choices that were previously left open auditable before data collection: cell identity, protocol conditions, allocation, measurement settings, reference procedures, model comparisons, and decision rules. The proposed 120-cell allocation is a planning starting point, not a substitute for the required simulation; enrollment must follow the preregistered precision analysis and available resources. Cell-level splitting, batch representation across protocols, and complete exclusion of protocol 2 from training distinguish performance on new cells from performance under the tested protocol shift. They do not establish generalization to other protocols, manufacturers, or chemistries.

Capacity measurements provide the SOH reference, while independent electrode diagnostics limit circularity in mechanism evaluation. Explicitly treating unmeasured or uncertain mechanism labels as indeterminate avoids transferring labels from a destructive subsample without evidence. Cell-grouped calibration and confidence intervals account for repeated checkpoints, while the stated exchangeability limitation makes clear that held-out-protocol coverage may fail under distribution shift.

The pilot and resource accounting address feasibility: they test acquisition time and quality-control yield before committing study cells and make instrument and aging burdens visible. Prespecified practical accuracy and trade-off criteria give the results an interpretable decision threshold. If sample size or reference labels are inadequate, the study still yields a valid SOH comparison but must present subgroup coverage and mechanism classification as exploratory rather than overstating precision.

Clarity.review: The experiment is clearly organized and closely aligned with the research question. It specifies the cell scope, aging protocols, allocation and holdout logic, EIS acquisition, SOH reference, mechanism-label rules, model comparisons, uncertainty assessment, and practical-use criteria. The rationale also makes the limits of transfer and the risks of sparse mechanism labels explicit. Together, these details make the intended setup and interpretation understandable and largely reproducible.
Clarity.feedback: A few choices still need to be made numerical and operational in the preregistration: the two aging protocols and operating envelope; rapid-band frequencies and acquisition-time limit; checkpoint schedule; quality-control thresholds; and the simulation assumptions and precision targets that determine final enrollment. Clarify how cells and checkpoints are sampled for destructive testing, and how cell-level conformal scores and cell-weighted metrics are calculated when cells have different numbers of valid observations. Also specify the intended application used to set acceptable MAE and the allowed difference from full-spectrum EIS. These are requirements for finalizing the protocol rather than major gaps in its description.

Validity.review: The design is strongly aligned with the research question and has good safeguards against data leakage, circular mechanism labeling, and pseudoreplication. It distinguishes performance on new cells from transfer to the second tested protocol, compares rapid-band EIS with relevant alternatives, and treats uncertainty and practical utility as testable outcomes rather than assuming success. Its conclusions are appropriately bounded to the specified cell type, protocols, and operating envelope.
Validity.feedback:
The main limitation is that protocol 2 is also the held-out-protocol test: protocol effects cannot be disentangled from protocol-specific cohort or other condition differences, and one held-out protocol provides only a narrow test of transfer. Batch allocation across protocols helps, but the study should ensure batches and other relevant factors are balanced in both training and test splits, and describe the result as transfer between these specific conditions.

The 120-cell allocation is appropriately provisional, but the precision simulation needs to account for the clustered checkpoint structure and the expected number of cells with usable mechanism labels. Requiring 20 determinate cases per class in each held-out test may be difficult given destructive sampling and indeterminate labels; the protocol should show that the planned sampling can meet this threshold or explicitly treat mechanism validation as exploratory. Also clarify how the “applicable independent diagnostic evidence” condition can be met for cells without harvested-cell confirmation, so the classifier’s decision rule is operational and does not inadvertently restrict calls to a selectively verified subset.

Finally, specify how capacity-test error and any baseline-capacity drift are handled in the SOH target and its uncertainty. For conformal intervals, state the precise cell-level score and coverage estimand: cell-level calibration supports a different guarantee from checkpoint-level marginal coverage, especially under protocol shift. These points are addressable and do not undermine the core design, but they affect interpretation of mechanism and calibration results.

Robustness.review: The design is unusually strong on robustness within its stated scope. It prespecifies the cell-level split, a genuinely held-out protocol, batch blocking, measurement quality controls, independent SOH and mechanism references, matched baselines, and cell-aware uncertainty estimates. It also appropriately limits claims: two protocols and one cell type cannot establish general transfer across chemistries, manufacturers, or field conditions.
Robustness.feedback: The main remaining risks are practical and inferential. First, the proposed 120-cell allocation may be inadequate for precise protocol-level coverage estimates or mechanism classification, especially after attrition and indeterminate labels. The simulation should explicitly target precision for each primary held-out comparison and interval coverage, not just overall SOH error; treat the 20-cell protocol-1 holdout as potentially underpowered for subgroup claims. Second, clarify how destructive reference labels align with repeated checkpoints and test cases: the plan appropriately avoids extrapolating labels, but this may leave few independently labeled cases for confirmatory mechanism evaluation. Third, cell-level conformal calibration does not by itself ensure nominal coverage under protocol shift; report protocol-2 coverage as an empirical transport test and avoid interpreting a favorable estimate as a guarantee. Finally, preregister the exact cell-weighted aggregation, bootstrap resampling unit, and handling of missing measurements so these choices cannot change after results are seen. These are refinements to an already rigorous design, not fundamental gaps.

Feasibility.review: The experiment is feasible as a well-equipped laboratory study, and the design is substantially more operationally specified than a typical EIS validation proposal. The pilot, explicit acquisition and quality-control rules, cell-level splits, independent capacity reference, and cautious handling of mechanism labels all reduce the risk of an uninterpretable result. The main constraints are substantial: long aging and repeated temperature/SOC measurements consume cycler and instrument time, and destructive electrode balancing is labor-intensive and may yield too few determinate labels for the planned confirmatory mechanism tests. The proposed 120 cells should therefore be treated strictly as a provisional allocation; achieving the precision targets or 20 determinate cases per class in each holdout may require considerably more cells.
Feasibility.feedback: Before enrollment, translate the measurement schedule into a resource budget: expected cycles and duration per protocol, EIS and capacity-test hours per cell, chamber and cycler capacity, staffing for harvesting and half-cell analysis, and contingency for attrition or failed spectra. Confirm that batch representation and the held-out-protocol split are feasible with the selected cell supply; if protocol and batch cannot be separated, narrow the transfer claim accordingly. Specify how destructive-testing selection relates to the held-out sets so the mechanism test remains independent and sufficiently powered. Finally, define the practical MAE and permitted increase over full-spectrum EIS from the intended application, and verify through simulation that the planned cell-level calibration and bootstrap analyses can estimate coverage and performance with useful precision. These are significant but manageable planning risks, not fundamental barriers.

Reproducibility.review: The design is highly reproducible at the protocol and analysis-plan level. It specifies cell identity, aging allocation, measurement and quality-control requirements, capacity reference, mechanism-label rules, cell-level splits, model comparisons, uncertainty calibration, and reporting expectations. The rationale also appropriately limits claims to the tested cell type and protocols, and avoids treating repeated checkpoints or unmeasured mechanism labels as independent or definitive evidence.
Reproducibility.feedback: The remaining reproducibility gaps are mostly implementation details that should be fixed in the preregistration before enrollment. Specify the exact aging schedules and numeric operating conditions, frequency grids and EIS settings, capacity-test procedure, and diagnostic fitting thresholds; the design requires these but does not provide their values. Define the precise cell-weighted aggregation and bootstrap procedure, conformal score and interval construction, classifier and feature-extraction algorithms, tuning budget, and practical-use margins. Clarify whether the stated 40 protocol-2 cells are all excluded from training (as implied) and how batch allocation and any protocol-2 cell holdout are handled. Finally, the 20-per-class criterion may be difficult to satisfy after stratified destructive sampling and indeterminate labels; show the simulation includes expected determinate counts per split and class, not just total enrollment. These details do not undermine the design’s structure, but are necessary for another lab to reproduce the exact implementation.

problems.problem: Can a temperature- and SOC-aware, uncertainty-calibrated EIS model estimate both lithium-ion battery SOH and its dominant degradation mode from brief, partial-frequency measurements collected under real operating conditions, while generalizing across cells and aging protocols?
problems.rationale: The target review highlights the need to connect EIS features to aging mechanisms and improve practical SOH evaluation. The related studies demonstrate fast EIS acquisition, SOH prediction from impedance features, and compensation for temperature and SOC, but generally address these factors separately or focus on SOH alone. Comparisons with incremental-capacity and differential-voltage analysis also suggest that EIS can inform degradation-mode diagnosis, though this has not yet been established as a robust, deployable inference task. A feasible study could collect EIS and reference capacity measurements across cells, temperatures, SOCs, and aging protocols; use partial-frequency spectra to reflect practical measurement constraints; and validate predictions on held-out cells and protocols. Reporting calibrated uncertainty alongside SOH and degradation-mode estimates would show when the model can be trusted by a battery-management system, and where broader validation is still needed.

Clarity.review: The problem is clearly framed as a prediction task: estimate both SOH and dominant degradation mode from partial-frequency EIS, accounting for temperature and SOC, with uncertainty calibration and cross-cell/protocol generalization. The rationale connects this scope to the cited work and identifies a practical gap. However, several terms leave the study boundaries open: “brief” measurements, “real operating conditions,” “dominant degradation mode,” and “uncertainty-calibrated” are not operationally defined. The question also combines multiple substantial objectives, making it unclear whether the central contribution is joint diagnosis, robustness to operating conditions, measurement speed, or uncertainty estimation.
Clarity.feedback: Specify the frequency range or measurement-time target for “brief,” define the operating conditions and degradation modes to be distinguished, and state how SOH and uncertainty will be measured and evaluated. Clarify the validation split and what counts as generalization across cells and aging protocols. This would make the scope and success criteria more reproducible.

Relevance.review: The problem is highly relevant to lithium-ion battery diagnostics and builds directly on the cited work in fast EIS acquisition, temperature/SOC compensation, SOH estimation, and degradation-mode analysis. Its combination of partial-frequency measurements, cross-cell and cross-protocol validation, and calibrated uncertainty addresses practical gaps that individual studies often treat separately. The focus on real operating conditions also strengthens its potential value for battery-management systems.
Relevance.feedback: The scope is ambitious: jointly estimating SOH and degradation mode under changing conditions is harder than SOH prediction alone, and degradation modes may not be uniquely identifiable from partial EIS spectra. Define the modes and independent reference labels clearly, control for confounding factors such as temperature and SOC, and compare against full-spectrum and established diagnostic baselines. Specify how uncertainty calibration and generalization will be evaluated; held-out cells and protocols are essential to support claims of deployment relevance. With these safeguards, the problem offers a meaningful and testable contribution.

Originality.review: The problem is well grounded in the cited work and combines several practical challenges: partial-frequency EIS, real operating conditions, joint SOH and degradation-mode estimation, uncertainty calibration, and generalization across cells and aging protocols. The combination is meaningfully more specific than SOH-only estimation or studies that compensate for temperature and SOC separately. However, its originality is primarily integrative rather than clearly foundational: fast EIS, environmental compensation, degradation diagnosis, and machine-learning-based health prediction each have substantial prior work. The supplied references do not establish whether their combination, or calibrated uncertainty for this task, has already been investigated.
Originality.feedback: Strengthen the novelty claim with a targeted comparison against prior work on joint SOH and degradation-mode inference, partial-frequency measurements under varying temperature and SOC, and cross-protocol validation. Define degradation modes and the independent evidence used to label them; impedance alone may not uniquely distinguish mechanisms. Specify what “real operating conditions” and “uncertainty-calibrated” mean, and compare against full-spectrum and SOH-only baselines. These choices would make the contribution testable and clarify whether it is a new inference capability or a careful integration of existing methods.

Feasibility.review: The problem is well motivated and grounded in existing EIS work, but it combines several difficult objectives: rapid partial-frequency measurement, compensation for temperature and SOC, estimation of both SOH and degradation mode, calibrated uncertainty, and generalization across cells and aging protocols. Each objective is plausible individually; demonstrating them together under real operating conditions is substantially harder.
Feasibility.feedback:
A controlled study is feasible, but its success depends on access to a sufficiently broad, well-characterized dataset. It needs multiple cells and aging protocols, reference capacity measurements, and credible labels for degradation modes, which can be difficult to obtain because real cells may exhibit overlapping degradation mechanisms. Partial-frequency data and operational variability may further reduce identifiability. Uncertainty calibration also needs evaluation under distribution shift, not just random held-out samples.

Narrow the initial scope: specify the chemistries and degradation modes, define the operating conditions and meaning of “brief,” and use held-out cells and protocols for validation. Compare against full-spectrum EIS and established diagnostics, and treat degradation-mode output as conditional on whether the available measurements support that distinction. With those constraints and suitable data access, the study is realistically investigable, though broad claims of deployment readiness would require further validation.

Significance.review: The problem addresses an important gap between laboratory EIS-based battery diagnostics and deployment in battery-management systems. Estimating SOH together with degradation mode from brief, partial-frequency measurements under varying temperature and SOC could advance both diagnostic capability and practical monitoring. Cross-cell and cross-protocol validation, paired with calibrated uncertainty, are particularly relevant because they test whether predictions are reliable beyond the conditions in which a model was developed.
Significance.feedback: The rationale is well grounded in the cited work, but the contribution depends on making degradation-mode labels and validation credible. Degradation modes can coexist and may be difficult to distinguish from impedance measurements alone; the study should specify how modes will be independently identified, how mixed or ambiguous cases will be handled, and what “uncertainty-calibrated” means operationally. It should also define the intended operating envelope and compare against appropriate baselines, including full-frequency EIS and existing voltage/current or incremental-capacity diagnostics. These details would clarify whether the work offers a deployable diagnostic advance or mainly an incremental modeling improvement.

problems.problem: For one lithium-ion cell chemistry and two controlled aging protocols, can EIS measurements limited to a predefined rapid frequency band estimate capacity-based state of health (SOH) across specified temperature and state-of-charge (SOC) ranges, and identify loss of lithium inventory (LLI) versus loss of active material (LAM) only when supported by independent reference diagnostics? Evaluate performance on cells and one aging protocol excluded from training, against full-spectrum EIS, SOH-only EIS models, and established voltage/current or incremental-capacity diagnostics. Does prediction uncertainty remain calibrated on these held-out data, as measured by coverage of prespecified prediction intervals?
problems.rationale: The target review calls for stronger links between EIS, aging mechanisms, and practical SOH estimation. Prior studies establish fast EIS acquisition, temperature/SOC compensation, and impedance-based SOH prediction; other work compares EIS with incremental-capacity and differential-voltage analysis for diagnosing degradation. The proposed study brings these threads together but narrows the scope to make the claims testable: one chemistry, two aging protocols, a predefined measurement band and operating envelope, and validation on unseen cells and a protocol. Capacity measurements provide the SOH reference, while independent diagnostic evidence provides LLI/LAM labels. Because degradation mechanisms can coexist or be indistinguishable from partial EIS, the model should report a mode only when reference-supported labels and measurement evidence permit it, otherwise returning “ambiguous.” Comparing with full-spectrum and established diagnostic baselines will show the cost of faster measurements; prediction-interval coverage on held-out data will test whether reported uncertainty is reliable beyond the training conditions.

Clarity.review: The problem is clearly framed as a bounded, testable study. It specifies the cell chemistry scope, aging protocols, rapid EIS constraint, operating conditions, capacity-based SOH target, degradation-mode distinction, held-out validation, comparison baselines, and uncertainty-calibration measure. The rationale connects these choices to the cited research landscape and appropriately recognizes that partial-spectrum EIS may not distinguish coexisting degradation mechanisms.
Clarity.feedback: Clarify what “predefined rapid frequency band” means, including its frequency limits and how the band is selected. Define the capacity-based SOH formula and the reference diagnostics used to label LLI and LAM. Also specify what “one aging protocol excluded from training” means for the split and whether results must generalize to both held-out cells and that protocol. Finally, identify the prediction-interval levels and the criterion for acceptable calibration. These details would make the evaluation more reproducible without changing the problem’s scope.

Relevance.review: The problem is strongly relevant to current EIS-based battery health research. It connects directly to work on rapid impedance acquisition, temperature/SOC effects, SOH prediction, and comparisons with incremental-capacity and voltage-based diagnostics. Its focus on held-out cells and an unseen aging protocol addresses a meaningful limitation of many estimation studies: performance that does not generalize beyond the training data. Separating capacity-based SOH evaluation from mechanism labels supported by independent diagnostics is also appropriately cautious, particularly given that partial-band EIS may not uniquely distinguish LLI from LAM.
Relevance.feedback: The scope is well defined and the proposed baselines make the practical trade-off between measurement speed and diagnostic performance testable. Specify the frequency band and acquisition-time target in advance, and define how cells and protocols are split to prevent leakage. Prespecify the uncertainty-calibration metric and acceptable coverage tolerance, alongside point-prediction metrics. Also clarify which independent diagnostics establish LLI/LAM labels and how mixed or uncertain labels are handled. These details will make the claims about generalization, mechanism identification, and calibrated uncertainty more interpretable.

Originality.review: The problem is well grounded in the cited literature and is more specific than a general proposal for EIS-based SOH estimation. Fast EIS acquisition, temperature/SOC effects, impedance-based prediction, and comparisons with incremental-capacity or voltage-differential methods have all been studied. The potentially distinctive contribution is to test a predefined rapid frequency band under protocol-held-out validation, pair capacity-based SOH with independently supported degradation labels, allow an “ambiguous” mechanism outcome, and assess prediction-interval calibration on held-out data. These choices make the study’s claims more rigorous and practically relevant, though they appear to be a careful synthesis and evaluation of established directions rather than a clearly unprecedented research question.
Originality.feedback: Specify how the rapid frequency band and operating envelope will be selected without using held-out data, and define the independent diagnostics and criteria used to assign LLI/LAM labels or mark cases ambiguous. Clarify the number and diversity of cells, how the excluded protocol tests generalization rather than a protocol-specific shift, and which baselines will be matched for training data and tuning. Prespecify calibration metrics and interval construction; empirical coverage alone can be misleading without interval width and adequate held-out sample size. These details will determine whether the combined validation design yields a substantive contribution beyond prior fast-EIS and degradation-diagnosis studies.

Feasibility.review: The problem is well scoped and experimentally testable. Its aims are supported by the cited research directions: rapid EIS acquisition, operating-condition compensation, SOH prediction, and comparison with established degradation diagnostics. Limiting the study to one chemistry, two aging protocols, and a predefined temperature/SOC envelope makes the data collection and validation more manageable. Capacity provides a clear SOH reference, while the requirement for independent diagnostics appropriately limits claims about LLI and LAM. Held-out cells and an entirely held-out protocol offer a meaningful test of generalization, and prediction-interval coverage adds a concrete check on uncertainty calibration.
Feasibility.feedback: The main feasibility risks are access to enough cells and the time and cost required to age them, especially if one complete protocol is reserved for testing. Specify the cell count, aging endpoints, EIS band and acquisition conditions, independent reference methods for labeling LLI/LAM, and the criteria for returning “ambiguous.” Ensure the baselines receive comparable training data and operating-condition information. Calibrating prediction intervals on a sufficiently large calibration set may be difficult when the test protocol is genuinely unseen; prespecify how calibration will be assessed and avoid implying that coverage on one held-out protocol establishes broad reliability. The proposed work is feasible, but its strength will depend on experimental replication and disciplined limits on mechanism claims.

Significance.review: The problem is significant and well grounded in the EIS battery-diagnostics literature. It addresses a practical obstacle to deploying EIS for battery management: whether faster, limited-band measurements can deliver reliable SOH estimates across operating conditions and generalize to unseen cells and aging protocols. Its comparison with full-spectrum EIS and established diagnostics makes the speed–accuracy tradeoff assessable. The cautious treatment of LLI/LAM, including an “ambiguous” outcome when evidence is insufficient, also avoids overstating what impedance data can establish. Calibrated prediction intervals add useful evidence about reliability beyond average prediction error.
Significance.feedback: The scope is appropriately constrained, but the contribution depends on clearly defining the frequency band, temperature/SOC envelope, cell-level and protocol-level data splits, and the independent diagnostics used to assign LLI/LAM labels. Specify interval-coverage targets and how coverage will be assessed; with limited held-out data, apparent calibration may be imprecise. Also clarify whether “unseen protocol” means an entire protocol is held out, since that is a stronger generalization test than holding out cells from protocols represented in training. These details will determine whether the results support practical deployment or only feasibility for the tested chemistry and conditions.

methods.method:
Conduct a preregistered, blinded study using replicate cells of one specified lithium-ion chemistry, assigned to two controlled aging protocols. Before collecting outcome data, define the rapid EIS frequency band, measurement procedure, operating envelope, and analysis plan. At scheduled aging checkpoints, measure EIS within that band and across the full spectrum, at prespecified temperature and SOC combinations. Standardize equilibration and acquisition, repeat a subset of measurements to quantify instrument and within-cell variability, and apply prespecified data-quality checks such as Kramers–Kronig consistency.

Use capacity measured under a fixed reference procedure as the SOH target. Obtain LLI/LAM reference labels independently of the EIS model, using prespecified diagnostic measurements and analysis; retain mixed or indeterminate cases rather than forcing them into a single class. Split data by cell and aging protocol before model selection: reserve entire cells and one protocol for the final held-out evaluation, and prevent measurements from the same cell appearing across training and test sets.

Train a rapid-band model that predicts SOH and its predictive interval while accounting for temperature, SOC, cell-level variation, and repeated measurements. Separately train a mechanism classifier using only reference-supported labels. It may return LLI or LAM only when the relevant reference label is available and the model’s prespecified evidence and confidence criteria are met; otherwise it returns “ambiguous.” Tune all model and decision thresholds using training data only.

Compare the rapid-band approach with: (1) full-spectrum EIS models, (2) EIS models predicting SOH without mechanism classification, and (3) voltage/current and incremental-capacity/differential-voltage baselines, evaluated using the same cell-level splits and reference outcomes. Report held-out SOH error and bias, mechanism-classification performance on labeled cases plus the ambiguous fraction, and empirical coverage and width of prespecified prediction intervals. Include calibration plots and subgroup results across the defined temperature and SOC ranges. Treat the protocol-held-out results as the primary test of transfer; do not use them to select models or thresholds.
methods.rationale:
The study tests the practical trade-off between rapid acquisition and diagnostic information while addressing the limitations highlighted by the reviews: EIS depends on operating conditions, impedance features do not uniquely identify degradation mechanisms, and reported estimation accuracy may not transfer beyond the conditions used for training. Fixed acquisition conditions and explicit temperature/SOC coverage make the scope reproducible; cell- and protocol-level holdouts reduce leakage and test generalization to new cells and aging conditions.

Independent capacity measurements anchor SOH, while independent mechanism diagnostics avoid circularly validating EIS against labels inferred from EIS itself. Allowing mixed or ambiguous outcomes reflects the fact that LLI and LAM can coexist and may not be separable from a partial spectrum. Matched baselines quantify what is gained or lost by restricting the frequency band and by adding mechanism prediction. Finally, held-out interval coverage tests whether uncertainty estimates remain reliable under distribution shift, rather than relying on point accuracy alone.

Clarity.review: The method is clearly organized and addresses the research problem directly. It specifies the study design, measurement conditions, independent SOH and mechanism references, cell- and protocol-level data separation, comparator models, and held-out evaluation metrics. The rationale also explains why ambiguity is retained for mechanism predictions and why protocol-held-out performance is the primary transfer test. This is enough to understand the study’s structure, but not yet enough to reproduce it precisely.
Clarity.feedback: Specify the chemistry, aging protocols, sample size and replicate allocation, checkpoint schedule, frequency band and full-spectrum settings, temperature/SOC grid, equilibration criteria, and reference-capacity procedure. Define the diagnostic measurements and analysis used to assign LLI/LAM labels, including how mixed cases are handled. Also name the model families, feature processing, interval method and nominal coverage levels, decision thresholds, and data-quality acceptance criteria. Clarify how the held-out cells and protocol can be evaluated without training on that protocol, particularly if its cells also need to be reserved for a distinct cell-level test. These details would make the plan substantially more reproducible and clarify the intended scope of generalization.

Validity.review: The method is well aligned with the research problem and the cited literature. It directly tests rapid-band EIS against full-spectrum EIS and established diagnostic baselines, uses capacity measured independently as the SOH reference, and avoids treating impedance alone as definitive evidence of LLI or LAM. Preregistered acquisition conditions, repeated measurements, cell-level separation, and a protocol-held-out primary test strengthen reproducibility and reduce leakage. Reporting interval coverage and width, subgroup performance, and the fraction classified as ambiguous also makes the evaluation more informative than point accuracy or forced mechanism classification alone.
Validity.feedback: Specify the chemistry, aging protocols, frequency band, operating envelope, sample size, reference capacity procedure, and independent LLI/LAM diagnostics before preregistration; these details determine whether the study is reproducible and adequately powered. Clarify how the held-out protocol is handled alongside training: with only two protocols, protocol-level transfer testing is inherently limited and may confound protocol effects with other differences between cohorts. Define the prediction-interval method and prespecified coverage targets, and assess calibration separately by relevant subgroups; aggregate coverage can conceal miscalibration under distribution shift. Also specify how repeated measurements and cell-level variation enter evaluation so the effective sample size is not overstated. Finally, make clear that mechanism performance is evaluated only for reference-labeled cases, and report how ambiguous and mixed cases affect interpretation.

Rigorousness.review:
The method is well aligned with the research problem and is substantially more rigorous than a typical exploratory EIS study. Preregistration, fixed measurement conditions, independent reference outcomes, cell-level separation, and a protocol-held-out primary test address major risks of leakage, circular validation, and overclaiming mechanism identification. The comparison set and reporting of SOH error, bias, classification performance, ambiguity, and interval coverage are also appropriate.

Some design details remain underspecified. The protocol-held-out evaluation may be confounded if protocol effects coincide with differences in cell batch, temperature/SOC exposure, or aging severity; the study should specify replication and control these factors where feasible. “Evidence and confidence criteria” for mechanism calls need operational definitions, and the independent LLI/LAM diagnostics should include their uncertainty and rules for mixed or indeterminate labels. For uncertainty calibration, prespecify the interval construction, nominal coverage levels, and how coverage will be assessed with clustered repeated measurements; calibration plots alone do not establish reliable coverage. Finally, define the primary SOH metric and comparisons, handle missing or failed measurements, and ensure baseline models receive comparable tuning and information without access to held-out data.
Rigorousness.feedback: Keep the scope narrow, but make the estimands and decision rules explicit before data collection. Report cell counts and power or precision targets, account for repeated observations at the cell level, and distinguish performance on labeled mechanism cases from coverage of all cases, including ambiguous ones. These additions would make the transfer and calibration claims more interpretable.

Innovativeness.review: The method’s main contribution is a rigorous, integrated evaluation design rather than a clearly new EIS measurement or modeling technique. Rapid-band EIS, operating-condition compensation, SOH prediction, degradation-mode analysis, and conventional diagnostic comparisons are all established research directions in the cited literature. Combining them with independent mechanism labels, cell- and protocol-level holdouts, and prespecified uncertainty-coverage tests creates a more credible and practically relevant assessment than a typical accuracy-focused study. The “ambiguous” mechanism outcome is also a sound way to avoid overstating what partial-spectrum measurements can identify.
Innovativeness.feedback: The proposed controls make the claims testable and reduce leakage, circular validation, and overclaiming. However, the method does not specify a novel model, frequency-band selection principle, or calibration procedure; its methodological innovation is primarily in the study design and synthesis of existing approaches. Strengthen the innovation claim by specifying how the rapid band is selected before outcome data are collected and what modeling or calibration approach handles cell variation and protocol shift. Also define the independent LLI/LAM diagnostics and their limitations, since the credibility of mechanism results depends on those reference labels.

Generalizability.review: The method is designed with generalizability in mind: cell-level separation prevents leakage, and holding out an entire aging protocol provides a meaningful test of transfer to an unseen aging condition. Prespecified operating conditions, independent reference measurements, matched baselines, and evaluation of prediction-interval coverage further strengthen the assessment. However, the scope remains deliberately narrow: one chemistry, two controlled protocols, and a defined temperature/SOC envelope. A single held-out protocol offers limited evidence for transfer to other chemistries, cell designs, manufacturers, or real-world duty cycles. The method tests generalization rigorously within its chosen setting, but does not establish broad applicability.
Generalizability.feedback: State explicitly that conclusions apply only to the tested chemistry and operating envelope. Where feasible, include additional protocols or external cells from another source to test transfer beyond the study cohort. Report performance by relevant subgroups and distinguish protocol transfer from shifts in temperature, SOC, cell design, or measurement equipment. Ensure the split leaves enough independent cells and reference-labeled cases for reliable estimates, and prespecify how calibration and ambiguous mechanism predictions will be assessed on held-out data.

methods.method:
** Define the study’s scope before enrollment: one named cell chemistry and format, two controlled aging protocols, a fixed temperature/SOC envelope, and a rapid EIS band. Select that band using an engineering rule independent of SOH and mechanism outcomes: identify a contiguous frequency range that the intended instrument can acquire within a prespecified time limit and that spans the targeted electrochemical processes, using pilot or published data only. Freeze the band, acquisition settings, preprocessing, and analysis plan before collecting study outcomes. Treat findings as applying to this chemistry, format, instrument class, and operating envelope.

Use a randomized, blocked design with cells from at least two manufacturing batches allocated across both protocols, so protocol is not confounded with batch. Set cell counts by simulation-based power and precision analysis using the cell—not each measurement—as the independent unit; choose counts to estimate the primary SOH error and interval coverage with prespecified confidence-interval widths, and ensure enough independently reference-labeled cells for mechanism evaluation. Report the assumptions and resulting allocation in the preregistration. If only two protocols are feasible, describe protocol transfer as a test between these two conditions, not evidence of broad transfer to other aging regimes.

At fixed aging checkpoints, acquire rapid-band and full-spectrum EIS on the same cells. Preregister the frequency grid and perturbation settings for both measurements, temperature/SOC grid, and a maximum acquisition time for the rapid band. For each condition, equilibrate until cell temperature is within ±0.5 °C of target and open-circuit voltage changes by less than a prespecified threshold over a fixed monitoring window; record failures to reach equilibrium. Randomize measurement order where feasible, standardize rest periods, and repeat a subset to quantify repeatability. Accept spectra only when instrument-range checks pass and a preregistered linearity/stability and Kramers–Kronig residual criterion is met. Retain failed or missing observations in the study flow and report their reasons; do not impute failed spectra as valid measurements.

Define capacity-based SOH as measured discharge capacity divided by the cell’s initial reference capacity, under a fixed temperature, current, voltage limits, and rest procedure. Measure reference capacity at baseline and each checkpoint, with replicate tests at a prespecified subset of checkpoints to quantify reference error.

Assign mechanism labels without using EIS model outputs. Use a preregistered combination of reference diagnostics, such as half-cell electrode balancing from harvested cells, supported where available by coulombic-efficiency and differential-voltage/incremental-capacity analysis. State the diagnostic protocol, fitting procedure, uncertainty, and evidence threshold in advance. Classify cases as LLI-dominant or LAM-dominant only when the relevant diagnostic evidence exceeds that threshold and uncertainty excludes the competing interpretation; label co-occurring supported mechanisms as mixed, and insufficient or conflicting evidence as indeterminate. Evaluate classification performance only against determinate reference labels, while reporting mixed, indeterminate, and model-ambiguous fractions separately.

Separate data at the cell level before any feature selection or tuning. The primary transfer test uses the second aging protocol as a completely held-out protocol, with its cells excluded from fitting, feature selection, calibration, and threshold setting. Also reserve cells from the training protocol as a distinct held-out-cell test. Thus report two separate tests: new cells under a represented protocol, and a new protocol. If protocol and cohort differences remain inseparable, state that limitation. Use the training data only for model selection and threshold setting; use nested cell-grouped cross-validation within the training protocol for tuning.

For the rapid-band SOH model, use a preregistered, regularized hierarchical regression with temperature and SOC as covariates, cell-level random effects during training, and a fixed-effects prediction rule for unseen cells. Transform real and imaginary impedance components to log-magnitude/phase or a preregistered equivalent representation, standardize using training data only, and retain the same preprocessing for all EIS models. Construct 90% and 95% prediction intervals using a cell-grouped conformal calibration procedure on training data; do not recalibrate on held-out data. Report empirical coverage and interval width with cell-clustered confidence intervals, overall and by temperature, SOC, protocol, and SOH range. Include residual and calibration plots, but treat prespecified coverage estimates and their uncertainty as the calibration assessment.

Train a separate mechanism model only on determinate reference-labeled cases. Make an LLI or LAM call only if the predicted class probability exceeds a threshold fixed on training data and the corresponding reference-supported evidence condition is met; otherwise return “ambiguous.” Never force mixed or indeterminate references into a binary class. Report sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, and confusion matrices on determinate cases, alongside the proportion of all test cases called, mixed, indeterminate, or ambiguous.

Compare the rapid-band models with full-spectrum EIS models, SOH-only EIS models, and voltage/current and incremental-capacity/differential-voltage baselines. Give each baseline the same training cells, tuning budget, reference outcomes, and held-out splits; prohibit access to held-out labels or measurements during model selection. Prespecify primary SOH performance as cell-weighted mean absolute error, with RMSE and signed bias as secondary metrics. Aggregate repeated checkpoint measurements within cells for inferential uncertainty using cell-clustered bootstrap intervals, and report checkpoint-level results as descriptive rather than treating observations as independent. Report missingness and all exclusions by split.
